dvs: version your data files next to your code

Analysis projects pair code with data, and git is only good at half of that pairing. dvs keeps the data in the project tree, moves the bytes to shared storage, and gives git a few hundred bytes of metadata per file to track instead.

Documentation Source (A2-ai/dvs2)

Four verbs, two surfaces

Everything below is a real capture of dvs 0.4.0 running against a project with PK datasets. The same four verbs are available as a CLI and as an R package, and both operate on the same project interchangeably.

initpoint the project at a shared storage directory
addhash, compress, and store files; write metadata
statuscompare every tracked file against its metadata
getmaterialize missing files from storage, hash-verified

The loop

1. Initialize once per project

dvs init writes dvs.toml, the entire project configuration. It belongs in git; every clone reads the storage location from it.

2. Add data with a message

Each file is hashed (blake3), compressed (zstd), and stored once per unique content. Note the sizes: a 2.9 KB file stores as 842 B. The message travels with the data, like a commit message for a dataset.

3. Status knows three states

current matches the metadata, unsynced is on disk but modified, and absent is tracked but not on disk, the state every fresh clone starts in.

4. Get restores the rest

Retrieval is verified against the recorded hash before the file is moved into place; a re-add brings a modified file back to current.

What git tracks, what storage holds

In git

dvs.toml, one small JSON meta file per data file under .dvs/, and the .gitignore entries dvs wrote. A complete, versioned description of the data at kilobyte scale.

In storage

Content-addressed blobs, named by their hash, compressed, read-only, deduplicated across every project and user that shares the storage. Plus an append-only audit log of who added what, when.

The proof, from the session above: the meta file records the hash, git stages only metadata (no CSV in sight), and the blob sits in storage under its hash at a third of the original size:
